study.title: 2 Peter 3 - Watchful Hope before God's judgment and the new world
study.overview: Peter closes the letter reminding believers of the word already received through the prophets and the apostles, because the church would face mocking people who would deny the return of Christ. The chapter responds to this unbelief with three emphases: history already shows that God judges and intervenes; the time of God is not measured as ours; and the future hope must produce holy life, patience and spiritual growth. Thus the doctrine of Christ's return is not given for speculation, but for perseverance, purity, and worship.

outline.title: Remembrance of apostolic and prophetic teaching
outline.explanation: Peter says that he writes to awaken the sincere mind of the readers, reminding them of the words of the holy prophets and the commandment received from the apostles of the Lord and Saviour. The Christian faith is presented as a continuation of God's revelation, not as isolated novelty.

outline.title: The mockery of the wicked and the certainty of judgment
outline.explanation: The scoffers ridicule the promise of Christ's coming and act as if creation were immutable. Peter responds by remembering creation by the word of God, the flood and the fact that the present world is reserved for the fire and judgment of the wicked.

outline.title: The time of God, the divine patience and the holy life
outline.explanation: Peter corrects human reading of delay: for the Lord, one day and a thousand years are not the same measure as for us. The delay is patience, aiming at repentance. Therefore, believers must live in holiness, expecting new heavens and new earth, and seeking to be found in peace, without blemish.

outline.title: Paul, vigilance against the final error and doxology
outline.explanation: Peter interprets the Lord's patience as salvation and recognizes that some of Paul's letters are difficult and may be distorted by unstable people. He concludes by warning against deception and calling the church to grow in grace and knowledge of Christ, closing with glory to Jesus.

study.context: The chapter shows a Christian community already exposed to scoffers who questioned the promise of Christ's return. Peter responds both with biblical memory and pastoral exhortation: the same God who created and judged in the past remains sovereign over history. The notes provided indicate that Peter's argument relies on the prophets of the Old Testament, the teaching of the apostles, and the warning against false teachers. It is not necessary to assume more historical details than the text itself and the notes state.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites creation, judgment, repentance, and consummation. Creation proves that the world is not eternal in its present state and that God can transform the created order. The flood is remembered as a sign of real and past judgment. God's patience is not indifference, but a mercy that he calls repentance. The promise of new heavens and the new earth points to a complete renewal, in which righteousness dwells. Esschatology therefore has an ethical purpose: whoever expects the Lord's day must live in holiness, piety, peace and spiritual growth. The final doxology shows that all this hope culminates in Christ, to whom glory belongs.

scholarViews.insight: Peter closes by resuming his purpose: to protect readers from the false teachers to grow in grace, and ends with a doxology to Jesus Christ.
Peter uses the doctrine of Christ's return to believers to a life of purity and piety; biblical knowledge must produce holy practice.
The exhortation to grow in grace and knowledge shows that Christian life is a continuous process of spiritual maturity in Christ.

questions: If I really believe that the Lord will come back and judge the world, what in my routine needs to change today?
In which areas have I treated God's patience as a delay, rather than a repentance opportunity?
How can I grow concretely in grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ this week?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to three concrete attitudes: faithfully remember Scripture, live in holiness while awaiting Christ and resisting the deception that trivializes faith. A simple practice is to separate daily time for the Word and for examination of life, asking: Is my hope in the new heaven and the new earth producing more purity, patience and peace? It is also advisable to pray with a focus on repentance and growth, rather than just asking for immediate relief.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are partial and some comments were incomplete in the excerpt, especially in verses not mentioned directly by each commentator. The exact historical context of the recipients has not been detailed in the notes, so it is not appropriate to affirm it beyond what the chapter and excerpts support. It is also not possible to determine safely, only with these notes, whether the language of "new heavens and new earth" must be understood in an exclusively literal, symbolic or comprehensive way; the readings presented are interpretative.
